LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD only contains standard packaging logic: variable definitions, an `if` statement that selects `yq` as a build dependency (because `$_system_wasm_bindgen` is false), and a single VCS source entry (`git+https://github.com/ruffle-rs/ruffle.git#tag=$_channel-$_date`). No command substitution, `eval`, `curl`, `wget`, or other dynamic code runs at the top level or in `pkgver()`. The suspicious second `source` line overwrites the earlier entry that included `chromium-extension-ruffle.key`, leaving only the upstream git repository. Since no malicious network activity, file writes, or code execution occurs during `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` or `--printsrcinfo`, the build scripts are safe.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Safe; only standard VCS source and variable logic</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The `.SRCINFO` file contains only declarative package metadata for an Arch Linux AUR package (`chromium-extension-ruffle-nightly`). It lists dependencies, provides/conflicts, a source URL (`git+https://github.com/ruffle-rs/ruffle.git#tag=nightly-2026-08-27`), and a checksum. There is no executable code, script logic, network requests, or file modifications present in the file. All sources and options follow standard packaging conventions (e.g., using a pinned git tag, `options = !lto`). No obfuscation, base64, curl, eval, or other suspicious constructs are found. Therefore, the file does not exhibit any indicators of malicious behavior and appears safe.
</details>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard AUR PKGBUILD for building the Ruffle Flash Player emulator nightly packages. The source comes from the official Ruffle GitHub repository (ruffle-rs/ruffle). The package fetches upstream code via git, builds it using cargo/npm, and installs the resulting binaries and browser extensions. This is standard packaging workflow with no evidence of malicious behavior.

The `source` array has two declarations where the second overwrites the first (removing the `chromium-extension-ruffle.key` entry), but this is a simple configuration issue, not malicious code. The chromium extension package uses `jq` to generate a JSON manifest file piped to `install`, which is a legitimate packaging technique for browser extensions.

The `_date` variable is set to "2026-08-27", which is in the future relative to the current date (2025), but this is a metadata issue in the AUR package itself, not a supply chain attack. The build fetches from a tagged ref in the official Ruffle repository.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Standard AUR packaging for Ruffle emulator; no malicious activity detected.</summary>
</security_assessment>
